All examples on this page use the university wide table from the previous pages, with its canonical cover from the last page:

```
inst_dept(ID, name, salary, dept_name, building, budget)   -- instructor natural join department
Fc = { ID → name, salary, dept_name ;  dept_name → building, budget }
```

To run the queries below, first create the wide table as a view:

```sql
create view inst_dept as
select id, name, salary, dept_name, building, budget
from instructor natural join department;
```

## Lossless Join Decomposition

::: {.callout-note title="Key idea"}
If you split a table in two, you should be able to join the pieces back together and get *exactly* the original table back — not extra, made-up rows, and not missing ones.
:::

For $R$ decomposed into $R_1, R_2$, this must hold for every legal instance:

$$r = \pi_{R_1}(r) \bowtie \pi_{R_2}(r)$$

**Sufficient condition:** the decomposition is lossless if at least one of these is true:

$$R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_1 \quad \text{or} \quad R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_2$$

In other words: the attribute(s) shared between the two pieces must be enough, on their own, to act as a key for at least one of the two pieces.

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
This condition is sufficient whenever all our constraints are FDs. If other kinds of constraints are in play, it isn't guaranteed to be necessary.
:::

**Full checklist for a lossless decomposition:**

- $R_1 \cup R_2 = R$ — nothing gets left out
- $R_1 \cap R_2 \neq \phi$ — the two pieces actually share something in common
- $R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_1$ or $R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_2$ — that shared part is a key on at least one side

```{=html}
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>1 · cover R</b></div><span>R₁ ∪ R₂ = R</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>2 · overlap</b></div><span>R₁ ∩ R₂ ≠ ∅</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>3 · key test</b></div><span>R₁ ∩ R₂ → R₁ or R₂</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>all 3 hold</b></div><span>lossless</span></div></div>
```

### Worked Example: Splitting `inst_dept`

**A good split:** `instructor(ID, name, salary, dept_name)` and `department(dept_name, building, budget)` — exactly the dataset’s two real tables.

```{=html}
<div class="flow"><div class="box"><b>instructor</b><span>ID, name, salary, dept_name</span></div><div class="box grey"><b>department</b><span>dept_name, building, budget</span></div></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>Check</th><th>instructor ∩ department = {dept_name}</th><th>Holds?</th></tr><tr><td>R₁ ∪ R₂ = R</td><td>all six columns appear</td><td><span class="tick">✓</span></td></tr><tr><td>R₁ ∩ R₂ ≠ ∅</td><td>dept_name</td><td><span class="tick">✓</span></td></tr><tr><td>key test</td><td>dept_name → building, budget, so dept_name → department</td><td><span class="tick">✓</span></td></tr></table></div>
```

Joining the two pieces back gives exactly the original rows:

```sql
select count(*)
from (select distinct id, name, salary, dept_name from inst_dept) r1
     join (select distinct dept_name, building, budget from inst_dept) r2
     using (dept_name);
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>count</th></tr><tr><td>50</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row) · the same 50 rows as inst_dept</div>
```

**A bad split:** `R1(ID, name, dept_name)` and `R2(dept_name, salary, building, budget)`

The shared attribute is again `dept_name` — but now `dept_name` is not a key of `R2` (a department has many salaries) and not a key of `R1` (a department has many instructors). Projecting the data onto these two tables and joining them back on `dept_name` gives:

```sql
select count(*)
from (select distinct id, name, dept_name from inst_dept) r1
     join (select distinct dept_name, salary, building, budget from inst_dept) r2
     using (dept_name);
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>count</th></tr><tr><td>182</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row) · instead of 50</div>
```

Looking only at Biology, which has two instructors:

```{=html}
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>ID</th><th>name</th><th>salary</th><th>dept_name</th><th>row</th></tr><tr><td>80759</td><td>Queiroz</td><td>45538.32</td><td>Biology</td><td>original</td></tr><tr><td>80759</td><td>Queiroz</td><td>77036.18</td><td>Biology</td><td><b>spurious</b></td></tr><tr><td>81991</td><td>Valtchev</td><td>45538.32</td><td>Biology</td><td><b>spurious</b></td></tr><tr><td>81991</td><td>Valtchev</td><td>77036.18</td><td>Biology</td><td>original</td></tr></table></div>
```

The join matches *every* Biology instructor in `R1` with *every* Biology salary in `R2` — creating combinations that never existed in the original data. This decomposition is lossy, and it also fails to preserve `ID → salary`.

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
The lesson: it's not *whether* you split a table, it's *where* you split it. The same table can be decomposed well or badly.
:::

---

## Dependency Preservation

::: {.callout-note title="Key idea"}
After splitting a table, can you still check all your original rules just by looking at each piece separately — or do you need to join tables back together first to catch a rule violation? If you can check everything locally, the decomposition "preserves dependencies."
:::

Let $F_i$ be the set of FDs from $F^+$ that only involve attributes inside $R_i$. A decomposition into $R_1, ..., R_n$ **preserves dependencies** if:

$$(F_1 \cup F_2 \cup \cdots \cup F_n)^+ = F^+$$

If this fails, catching a violation of some original FD needs an expensive join across tables.

### A Quick Contrast

Same table `inst_dept`, same $F_c$:

```{=html}
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>Decomposition</th><th>Dependency Preserving?</th></tr><tr><td><code>instructor(ID, name, salary, dept_name)</code>, <code>department(dept_name, building, budget)</code></td><td>Yes — <code>ID → name, salary, dept_name</code> sits inside instructor and <code>dept_name → building, budget</code> inside department</td></tr><tr><td><code>R1(ID, name, salary, dept_name)</code>, <code>R2(ID, building, budget)</code></td><td>No — <code>dept_name → building</code> can’t be checked without joining, since <code>dept_name</code> and <code>building</code> now live in different tables (the split is still lossless: ID is a key of both)</td></tr></table></div>
```

Same relation, same FDs — the *choice* of split decides the outcome.

### How to Test It

1. Start with `result` set to just the left-hand-side attributes ($\alpha$) of the FD you're checking.
2. Go through each piece $R_i$ of the decomposition. Take the attributes `result` shares with $R_i$, compute their closure under the *full* $F$, then keep only the attributes that also belong to $R_i$. Add anything new to `result`.
3. Repeat step 2, cycling through every $R_i$, until `result` stops growing.
4. If the right-hand-side attributes ($\beta$) are now inside `result`, the FD is preserved without needing a join.

```{=html}
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>1 · start</b></div><span>result = α</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>2 · each Rᵢ</b></div><span>(result ∩ Rᵢ)⁺ ∩ Rᵢ</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>3 · repeat</b></div><span>until result stops growing</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>4 · β ⊆ result?</b></div><span>preserved</span></div></div>
```

Run this check on every FD in $F$ to confirm the whole decomposition preserves dependencies.

### Worked Example: an FD Spread Across Two Tables

Decomposition: `instructor(ID, name, salary, dept_name)`, `department(dept_name, building, budget)`.

`ID → budget` is in $F^+$, but `ID` and `budget` never sit in the same table. Is it still preserved?

```{=html}
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>Round</th><th>Piece Checked</th><th>Closure Computed</th><th>Result So Far</th></tr><tr><td>Start</td><td>—</td><td>—</td><td><code>{ID}</code></td></tr><tr><td>1</td><td>instructor</td><td>(ID)⁺ = every column, keep only instructor’s columns</td><td><code>{ID, name, salary, dept_name}</code></td></tr><tr><td>1</td><td>department</td><td>(dept_name)⁺ = dept_name, building, budget, keep department’s columns</td><td><code>{ID, name, salary, dept_name, building, budget}</code></td></tr></table></div>
```

`result` now contains `budget` — so `ID → budget` is preserved: checking `ID → dept_name` in `instructor` and `dept_name → budget` in `department` is enough.

### Worked Example: an FD That Is Lost

Decomposition: `R1(ID, name, salary, dept_name)`, `R2(ID, building, budget)`. Check `dept_name → building`:

```{=html}
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>Round</th><th>Piece Checked</th><th>Closure Computed</th><th>Result So Far</th></tr><tr><td>Start</td><td>—</td><td>—</td><td><code>{dept_name}</code></td></tr><tr><td>1</td><td>R1</td><td>(dept_name)⁺ = dept_name, building, budget, keep only R1’s columns</td><td><code>{dept_name}</code></td></tr><tr><td>1</td><td>R2</td><td>result ∩ R2 = {} → nothing to add</td><td><code>{dept_name}</code></td></tr></table></div>
```

`building` never enters `result`, so `dept_name → building` is **not preserved**. In practice: a new Biology instructor could be inserted into `R2` with building `Watson`, while the other Biology instructors say `Candlestick`. Neither table on its own breaks a rule; only a join of `R1` and `R2` reveals that Biology now has two buildings.
